LANDSCAPE AND VISUAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT
Introduction
The assessment of potential landscape and visual impacts due to construction and
operation of the Project is presented in this chapter.
Landscape and visual impacts were assessed in accordance with the criteria and
guidelines as stated in Annexes 10 and 18 of the Technical Memorandum on
Environmental Impact Assessment Process (EIAO-TM) and the latest version of
Environmental Impact Assessment ordinance (EIAO) Guidance Note No. 8/2023 on
“Preparation of Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment under the Environmental
Impact Assessment Ordinance”.
Scope and Content of the Study
Assessment Area
The assessment area for landscape impact assessment includes all areas within a
100m from the Project boundary in accordance with EIA Study Brief
(No. ESB-375/2025). The assessment area for the visual impact assessment is
defined by the visual envelope of the Project. The landscape impact study boundary
are shown in Figures 60722948/A10/FIGURE 10.1 to 10.7. The aerial photos overlaid
with the project layout are shown in Figures 60722948/A10/FIGURE 10.8 to 10.14.
Landscape Impact Assessment
The existing and planned landscape resources and character within the assessment
area were described, appraised, analysed and evaluated. A system is derived for
judging landscape and visual impact significance as required under the Technical
Memorandum. The sensitivity of the landscape framework and its ability to
accommodate change are particularly focused on. The degree of compatibility of the
Project with the existing and planned landscape setting was identified. The
landscape impact assessment evaluated the potential landscape impact so as to
illustrate the significance of such impacts arising from the Project. Clear mapping of
the baseline landscape resources, landscape character areas and the landscape
impact were provided.
Visual Impact Assessment
The visual impact of the Project was assessed. For aboveground structures of the
Project, clear illustrations including mapping of visual impact are provided. The
assessment adopts a systematic methodology and includes the following:-
• Identification and plotting of visual envelope of the Project;
• Appraisal of existing visual resources and character as well as the future outlook
of the visual system of the assessment area;
• Identification and justification of the key public viewing points within the visual
envelope and their views at sea level, ground level and elevated vantage points,
and clearly indicate the key public viewing points on a plan of appropriate scale;

Landscape and Visual Mitigation Measures
The merit of preservation in total or in parts of existing landscape and the
establishment of a new landscape character are evaluated. Alternative construction
methods and / or Project-related works or structure(s) that would avoid or reduce the
identified landscape and visual impacts are considered and evaluated for comparison
before adopting other mitigation or compensatory measures to alleviate the impacts.
The mitigation measures proposed are not only concerned with damage reduction
but also included consideration of potential enhancement of the existing landscape
and visual quality. Mitigation measures to minimise the adverse effects identified,
including provision of a landscape design, are recommended.
The mitigation measures such as tree preservation and tree transplanting as far as
practical, provision of buffer planting, reinstatement of affected landscape area,
compensatory planting, erection of decorative screen hoarding that compatible with
the surrounding setting, reprovision of amenity areas / open spaces, aesthetic design
and layout of structures and façade treatment etc. Parties are identified for the on-
going management and maintenance of the proposed mitigation works to ensure their
effectiveness throughout the operation of the Project. A practical programme and
funding proposal for the implementation of the recommended measures are provided.
Significance of Landscape and Visual Impact
Annotated illustration such as coloured perspective drawings, plans and
section/elevation diagrams, oblique aerial photographs, photographs taken at
vantage points and computer-generated photomontage are adopted where
appropriate to illustrate the significance of the landscape and visual impacts of the
aboveground ancillary structures of the Project.

Landscape Impact Assessment Methodology
The landscape impact was assessed according to the following procedures:-

on the Landscape Resources (LRs) and Landscape Character Areas (LCAs).

the Assessment area. The assessment area includes all areas within 100m
of the Project area. This is achieved by site visits and desktop study of
topographical maps, information databases and photographs.
• Assessment of the degree of sensitivity of the LRs and LCAs. This is
influenced by a number of factors including whether the resource/character is
common or rare, whether it is considered to be of local, regional, national or
global importance, whether there are any statutory or regulatory
limitations/requirements relating to the resource, the quality of the
resource/character, the maturity of the resource and the ability of the

A broad brush tree and vegetation survey was carried out to identify the existing trees
and vegetation located within the project area and account the baseline condition of
existing landscape resources at the time of EIA preparation. To quantify and
safeguard the quality of broad brush tree and vegetation survey information, on-site
survey at the nearest accessible areas in combination of aerial photo analysis and
drone technology was adopted. For accessible areas (such as roadside areas of LMC
and Ma Tso Lung), the tree and vegetation survey information was collected by on-
site visual inspection. For remaining areas with site constraints and
safety/accessibility problems (such as hillside locations and steep slopes, within
private lots and fence off areas etc.), the tree quantity and tree information estimation
were collected from aerial photos and drone photos of high resolution, with visual
inspection at the nearest locations to quantify the findings as far as possible.
Furthermore, existing trees would be carefully grouped in consideration of the extent
of each LR, within site/ outside site location, tree and vegetation composition and
density, accessibility and geographical location of the tree group etc. Therefore, the
conducted on-site broad brush tree and vegetation survey, in combination of aerial
photo and drone technology to increase the accuracy, provides representative tree
and vegetation information for effective analysis.
Based on the broad brush tree and vegetation survey information, approximately
2,642 nos. of trees were surveyed within the 100m assessment area. None of these
are Registered Old and Valuable Trees (OVTs). Dominant tree species include
Macaranga tanarius var. tomentosa, Celtis sinensis, Dimocarpus longan, Ficus
microcarpa, Pinus elliottii and Melia azedarach etc. that commonly found in Hong
Kong were identified. 5 nos. of Trees of Particular Interest (TPIs) are identified in
accordance with Section 3 of Appendix I of the EIA Study Brief No. ESB-375/2025.
For the 5 nos. of TPIs, 1 no. of Cinnamomum camphora is in large size with DBH
over 1m, and 4 nos. of Aquilaria sinensis with conservation interest under Cap. 586
are surveyed. A few numbers of undersized Aquilaria sinensis are also recorded in
Chapter 8 of EIA Report, the indicative location also reflected in the broad brush tree
and vegetation survey. The broad brush tree and vegetation survey including tree
and vegetation survey plans and tree schedule are illustrated in Appendix 10.1.

• Operation of the ECR, including carriageway and associated structures, etc.;

The magnitude of residual landscape impacts of LR3, LR4, LR6, LR7, LCA3,
